visualizations.title: Ward-Level Equity & Charging Deficit
visualizations.subtitle: Spatial disparity across 15 Pune Municipal Corporation administrative units
visualizations.key_takeaway: Hadapsar and Bhavani Peth have up to 483 EVs per charging point, creating acute geographic charging deserts.
data_meaning: Hadapsar (Ward 13) has 7,612 registered EVs but only 20 public stations (need score 85.5/100).
Bhavani Peth (Ward 12) exhibits a critical ratio of 483.3 EVs per charger, the highest in the entire district.
Historic core wards (Kasba Peth) have low geographic sprawl and <=100 EVs per station, demonstrating severe municipal misallocation.
Siting must strictly prioritize the eastern IT/industrial arc (Hadapsar, Kharadi, Wagholi) rather than central commercial corridors.

visualizations.title: Power Capacity & Charger Speed Mismatch
visualizations.subtitle: Analysis of 1,354 public charging points by kilowatt output and connector architecture
visualizations.key_takeaway: 86.9% of Pune's chargers are slow 3.3kW LEV points. Only 13.1% are fast DC chargers capable of servicing 4W passenger cars and commercial fleets.
data_meaning: Headline figures claiming 1,354 stations obscure the fact that 1,177 points are slow 3.3kW AC or light EV plugs.
A 3.3kW charger requires 4 to 8 hours for a full charge, making daytime replenishment impractical for ride-share fleets and commuters.
Only 177 verified charging stations offer >=7.4kW or DC fast charging (CCS-2 / CHAdeMO / Bharat DC-001).
This creates severe queue anxiety among EV cab and delivery drivers, proving the urgent need for high-speed multi-gun DC hubs.

visualizations.title: CPO Market Share & Private Dominance
visualizations.subtitle: Operator concentration and public vs private infrastructure ownership
visualizations.key_takeaway: Private operators account for 88.6% of charging points, with Ather dominating 2W AC and Tata Power dominating 4W DC.
data_meaning: Ather Energy maintains the largest footprint due to early rollout of proprietary LEV points in retail and restaurant locations.
Tata Power and ChargeZone provide the backbone of high-capacity highway and commercial DC fast charging.
Municipal and government utility deployments (MSEDCL / PMC) represent less than 12% of operational sites.
Lack of interoperability between proprietary CPO apps and billing networks creates severe user friction that municipal open-access hubs can resolve.

visualizations.title: Greedy Submodular Coverage Convergence
visualizations.subtitle: Mathematical proof of diminishing marginal returns across 20 siting iterations
visualizations.key_takeaway: Siting 10 stations achieves 90.0% citywide coverage (+6.5% gain). Stations 11-20 add only 1.7% combined, proving 10 is the optimal Pareto sweet spot.
data_meaning: Demonstrates the submodular property f(S U {x}) - f(S) >= f(T U {x}) - f(T) for S subset T, yielding an optimal greedy (1 - 1/e) guarantee.
The first 5 sited stations generate steep coverage improvements (+4.5%) by plugging major arterial deficits.
At k=10, the curve reaches an elbow point, reducing average distance citywide to 0.99 km.
Beyond k=10, marginal coverage gain drops below 0.3% per station, demonstrating that municipal CAPEX is best allocated to 10 strategic multi-gun hubs.

visualizations.title: Siting Decision Funnel & Criteria Correlation
visualizations.subtitle: Candidate reduction logic and trade-offs between arterial roads and deficit gaps
visualizations.key_takeaway: Filters 100 candidate intersections through 5 rigorous constraints to isolate the 10 highest-impact hubs.
data_meaning: Stage 1 generates 100 candidate nodes across Pune's road intersections, commercial centers, and transit nodes.
Stage 2 filters to 72 nodes within 200m of primary arterial roads with robust power feeder availability.
Stage 3 isolates 43 sites situated strictly within identified charging deserts (nearest charger >= 1.05 km).
Stage 4 ranks the top 21 candidates by composite need score, from which greedy submodular selection picks the final 10 with 1.15km spatial separation.

visualizations.title: EV Fleet Surge vs Infrastructure Deficit (2020-2026)
visualizations.subtitle: Longitudinal comparison of cumulative vehicle registrations and charging point growth
visualizations.key_takeaway: EV fleet size in Pune exploded 42-fold from 2020 to 2026, driving the EV-to-charger ratio from 347:1 down to ~195:1, still far above the 50:1 target.
data_meaning: Annual new EV registrations surged from 4,820 in 2020 to over 85,000 by 2025/2026, driven by Maharashtra's progressive EV subsidy policy.
Electric 2-wheelers represent >85% of registrations, but fast-charging demand is propelled heavily by commercial 4W cabs and delivery fleets.
While total public chargers grew from 18 to 1,354, the ratio remains at ~195 EVs per station—nearly 4x higher than NITI Aayog's recommended 50:1 limit.
Without proactive 60-120kW fast-charging corridor investments, grid bottlenecks will severely constrain Pune's net-zero mobility targets.
